q: Answer these questions about modern architects.
parts: Which Chinese-American architect designed the glass pyramid at the entrance of the Louvre?
Which Brazilian architect designed the government buildings of Brasilia, including the Cathedral with its hyperboloid form?
Which Iraqi-British architect, in 2004 the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize, designed the London Aquatics Centre?

q: Answer these questions about architectural terms.
parts: What term names the front face of a building?
What term names the triangular gable above a classical portico?
What term names a row of evenly spaced columns supporting a roofed walkway or entablature?

q: This ballet's second act features dances from Spain, Arabia, China, and Russia in the Land of Sweets. Its score includes the "Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy," which uses the celesta. Clara receives a wooden toy soldier on Christmas Eve and fights the Mouse King. For 10 points, name this Tchaikovsky ballet that is performed every December.

In this ballet, Prince Siegfried falls in love with Odette, a princess turned into a bird by the sorcerer Rothbart. The dual role of Odette and Odile is traditionally danced by one ballerina who performs thirty-two fouette turns. Tchaikovsky composed its score. For 10 points, name this ballet about a lake of enchanted birds.

In this ballet move, a dancer spins on one foot while the other leg is held in position such as passe or retire. A dancer can "spot" a fixed point with the head to avoid becoming dizzy. The name comes from a French word meaning "spin." For 10 points, name this turn in ballet and other dance forms.

This choreographer founded a modern dance company in 1926 and developed a technique based on contraction and release. Her works include Appalachian Spring, with music by Aaron Copland, and Lamentation. She danced with the Denishawn school before founding her own group. For 10 points, name this American pioneer of modern dance.

This choreographer founded a company in New York in 1958 to showcase African American dancers. His best-known work, Revelations, uses spirituals and blues to depict Black religious life. His company is based at the Joan Weill Center. For 10 points, name this American modern dance figure.

Burned down in 1613 when a cannon misfired during a performance of Henry VIII, this London playhouse was rebuilt. It had a round open-air design with a thrust stage and groundlings standing in the yard. It was home to the Lord Chamberlain's Men. For 10 points, name this theater associated with Shakespeare.

This Russian director and actor co-founded the Moscow Art Theatre in 1898. His acting "system" emphasized emotional memory and the actor's inner truth, and it influenced the American Method. He produced Chekhov's The Seagull. For 10 points, name this theater practitioner, Konstantin.

This form of improvised Italian theater from the sixteenth century used stock characters such as Harlequin, Pantalone, and Columbina. Performers wore masks and followed scenarios rather than scripts. It influenced Moliere and Punch and Judy. For 10 points, name this "comedy of the profession."

This Japanese theater form features all-male casts with elaborate costumes, dramatic makeup called kumadori, and stage devices such as the hanamichi, or "flower path," through the audience. It arose in the Edo period and was supposedly begun by a woman named Izumo no Okuni. For 10 points, name this theater form.

This Japanese theater form uses slow movement, masks such as hannya, and a chorus that comments on the action. Its plays are divided into categories such as god, warrior, woman, and demon plays. It was refined in the fourteenth century by Kan'ami and his son Zeami. For 10 points, name this classical drama, whose name means "skill."

In this musical, Aaron Burr sings "Wait for It," and King George III sings "You'll Be Back." Its cast sings and raps about a founder born in Nevis and a duel in Weehawken. It was written by and originally starred Lin-Manuel Miranda. For 10 points, name this musical about a first Treasury Secretary.

Set in New York City's Upper West Side, this musical's songs include "Maria," "Tonight," and "America." The score is by Leonard Bernstein with lyrics by Stephen Sondheim. The plot is loosely based on Romeo and Juliet and pits the Jets against the Sharks. For 10 points, name this 1957 musical.

This Andrew Lloyd Webber musical, set in the Paris Opera House, features a masked figure who haunts a soprano named Christine. Its title song features a pipe-organ riff, and a chandelier crashes in a famous scene. It is based on a novel by Gaston Leroux. For 10 points, name this longest-running Broadway show.

This German playwright developed "epic theater," in which the Verfremdungseffekt, or alienation effect, keeps audiences from being emotionally absorbed. His works include Mother Courage and Her Children and The Threepenny Opera, with music by Kurt Weill. He founded the Berliner Ensemble. For 10 points, name this dramatist.

This Japanese art form involves folding a single square sheet of paper into shapes such as cranes and frogs without cutting or gluing. A crane made of a thousand folded sheets is said to grant a wish. A flat square sheet is called kami. For 10 points, name this art whose name combines the words for "fold" and "paper."

This art of beautiful handwriting uses tools such as quills, brushes, and broad-edged pens. In China and Japan it is practiced with ink brushes, while in the Islamic world styles such as Kufic and Naskh decorate the Quran. For 10 points, name this art of decorative lettering.

This French performer created the character Bip, a clown in a battered top hat with a flower. He performed "The Cage" and "Walking Against the Wind" without speaking. He is the most famous practitioner of an art of silent gesture. For 10 points, name this mime, Marcel.

This Japanese puppet theater from Osaka uses large puppets, each operated by three people, with the principal puppeteer's face often visible. A chanter called a tayu voices all characters to the accompaniment of a shamisen. Chikamatsu wrote for it. For 10 points, name this traditional puppet theater.

Nicknamed "Bojangles," this performer danced a staircase routine in films with Shirley Temple, including The Little Colonel. His tap dancing was known for its light, upright style. He was famous on Broadway and in Hollywood in the 1920s and 1930s. For 10 points, name this tap dancer.

This Russian-born choreographer co-founded the School of American Ballet and the New York City Ballet. His works include Serenade and Jewels, and his Nutcracker became an annual tradition. He worked closely with Igor Stravinsky. For 10 points, name this choreographer.

This American playwright's Our Town is set in the fictional Grover's Corners, New Hampshire, and uses a Stage Manager as narrator with minimal scenery. He also wrote The Skin of Our Teeth and The Matchmaker, the basis for Hello, Dolly! For 10 points, name this dramatist who won three Pulitzer Prizes.

In this Greek tragedy by Sophocles, a plague strikes Thebes, and the king investigates the murder of his predecessor, Laius. The blind prophet Tiresias reveals that the king himself is the culprit. The king blinds himself after learning that he killed his father and married his mother. For 10 points, name this play.

This musical is based on a Victor Hugo novel set in nineteenth-century France. Its songs include "I Dreamed a Dream," "One Day More," and "Do You Hear the People Sing?" Jean Valjean is chased by Inspector Javert. For 10 points, name this musical, whose French title means "the miserable ones."

This songwriting duo wrote the musicals Oklahoma!, Carousel, South Pacific, and The Sound of Music. Their partnership began in 1943. One composed the music and the other the lyrics. For 10 points, name this pair, Richard and Oscar.

This impresario founded the Ballets Russes in 1909 and brought Vaslav Nijinsky and Anna Pavlova to Paris. He commissioned works from Stravinsky, including The Firebird and Petrushka, and from Ravel and Debussy. He also commissioned designs from Picasso and Matisse. For 10 points, name this Russian ballet company founder, Sergei.

Medieval artists made these images by cutting colored glass, fitting it into lead cames, and often adding painted details fired in a kiln. They fill the windows of Chartres and Sainte-Chapelle. Tiffany created many in America. For 10 points, name this art form that fills Gothic cathedral windows with colored light.

This kind of puppet is controlled from above by strings attached to a wooden crossbar. Pinocchio is a famous example. The name derives from the French for a small figure of the Virgin Mary. For 10 points, name this type of string puppet.

This Japanese art of arranging flowers emphasizes line, space, and asymmetrical balance, with three main elements representing heaven, earth, and humanity. It originated from offerings at Buddhist altars. For 10 points, name this art, which uses the words for "living flowers."

This musical by Andrew Lloyd Webber is based on whimsical poems by T. S. Eliot about the Jellicle tribe. Its song "Memory" is sung by Grizabella. It ran on Broadway for 18 years. For 10 points, name this musical with a feline cast.

In theater, this stage direction refers to the part of the stage farthest from the audience. The term arose when stages were raked, sloping upward toward the back. Actors who move toward the back of the stage are said to move this way. For 10 points, give this term, the opposite of downstage.

q: This 1765 act required colonists to buy stamped paper for newspapers, legal documents, and playing cards. Protests were led by groups such as the Sons of Liberty, and the slogan "no taxation without representation" spread. Parliament repealed it in 1766 but passed the Declaratory Act. For 10 points, name this British tax law.

In December 1773 colonists dressed as Mohawks boarded ships in Boston harbor and dumped 342 chests into the water. The protest was aimed at the Tea Act and the East India Company's monopoly. Parliament responded with the Intolerable Acts. For 10 points, name this event.

Horatio Gates commanded American forces at this 1777 battle in New York, where Benedict Arnold fought bravely. British General John Burgoyne surrendered his army afterward. The victory convinced France to ally with the United States. For 10 points, name this turning point of the American Revolution.

This first national government of the United States was ratified in 1781. It had a one-house Congress, no president, and no power to tax. Its weaknesses led to the Constitutional Convention in 1787. For 10 points, name this document that preceded the Constitution.

In 1786 and 1787 farmers led by a former Continental Army captain shut down courts in western Massachusetts to protest debts and taxes. Governor James Bowdoin raised a militia to put them down. The uprising helped convince leaders that the national government was too weak. For 10 points, name this revolt named for its leader Daniel.

President Thomas Jefferson bought land from France in 1803 for about 15 million dollars. Robert Livingston and James Monroe negotiated in Paris with Napoleon's government. The purchase roughly doubled the size of the United States. For 10 points, name this land deal that included New Orleans.

This 1819 Supreme Court case upheld the power of Congress to create the Second Bank of the United States under the necessary and proper clause. It also held that the state of Maryland could not tax the bank. Daniel Webster argued for the bank. For 10 points, name this case named for a Maryland official.

This first Secretary of the Treasury proposed that the federal government assume state debts and create a national bank. He wrote most of the Federalist Papers essays with John Jay and James Madison. He was killed in a duel in 1804 by Aaron Burr. For 10 points, name this man who appears on the ten-dollar bill.

This 1814 treaty ended the War of 1812 and returned things to their prewar status. It was signed in a city in Belgium. News of it had not yet arrived when Andrew Jackson won the Battle of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this treaty named for the city where it was signed.

This 1823 policy statement told European powers not to colonize or interfere in the Western Hemisphere. John Quincy Adams helped write it for a president from Virginia. The United States promised to stay out of European wars. For 10 points, name this doctrine.

This president signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830 and fought the Second Bank of the United States. His followers started the Democratic Party, and he won the Battle of New Orleans. His critics called him "King Andrew." For 10 points, name this seventh president, nicknamed "Old Hickory."

In the late 1830s about 16,000 Cherokee were forced to march west to present-day Oklahoma, and thousands died along the way. The removal followed the dubious Treaty of New Echota. The Supreme Court had ruled in Worcester v. Georgia that Georgia had no power over Cherokee land. For 10 points, name this forced march.

This woman escaped slavery in Maryland and made about thirteen trips back to the South as a conductor on the Underground Railroad. She later served as a Union scout and spy during the Civil War. She was known as "Moses." For 10 points, name this woman.

This 1848 treaty ended the Mexican-American War. Mexico gave up California and much of the Southwest in return for 15 million dollars. It was negotiated by Nicholas Trist. For 10 points, name this treaty, named for a town near Mexico City.

This 1850 package of laws admitted California as a free state and created a stricter Fugitive Slave Act. It was brokered by Henry Clay and Stephen Douglas. The slave trade was banned in the District of Columbia. For 10 points, name this compromise that delayed the Civil War.

This 1854 law created two territories and repealed the Missouri Compromise line by allowing popular sovereignty. It was championed by Stephen Douglas. It led to violence in "Bleeding Kansas" and helped spawn the Republican Party. For 10 points, name this act, named for two territories.

In this 1857 case Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled that African Americans could not be citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. The plaintiff had lived with his owner in Illinois and Wisconsin Territory. For 10 points, name this Supreme Court decision named for an enslaved man.

Fought in July 1863 in Pennsylvania, this Civil War battle saw Pickett's Charge fail on its third day. George Meade commanded the Union army against Robert E. Lee. Lincoln later dedicated a cemetery there. For 10 points, name this battle that turned the war against the Confederacy.

This order issued by Abraham Lincoln took effect on January 1, 1863. It declared enslaved people in Confederate-held areas to be free but did not apply to border states. It also allowed Black men to join the Union army. For 10 points, name this proclamation.

This agency of the War Department was created in 1865 to aid formerly enslaved people with food, schools, and labor contracts. It was led by General Oliver O. Howard, for whom a university in Washington is named. For 10 points, name this Reconstruction agency.

This 1862 law gave settlers 160 acres of public land if they lived on it and farmed it for five years. It was signed by Abraham Lincoln and brought many people to the Great Plains. For 10 points, name this act, named for a place to live.

In 1869 the Union Pacific and Central Pacific companies met at Promontory Summit in Utah. A ceremonial golden spike marked the completion. Irish and Chinese laborers did much of the work. For 10 points, name this feat of 1869.

This Harding administration scandal involved the secret leasing of oil reserves in Wyoming to private companies. Secretary of the Interior Albert Fall was convicted of accepting bribes. The scandal was named for a rock formation. For 10 points, name this scandal.

This 1906 novel by Upton Sinclair exposed horrible conditions in Chicago's meatpacking industry. Its publication helped lead to the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act. For 10 points, name this muckraking novel about Lithuanian immigrant Jurgis Rudkus.

This 1898 war began after the battleship Maine exploded in Havana harbor. The United States gained Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines. Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders fought at San Juan Hill. For 10 points, name this conflict with a European country.

This economic downturn began after the stock market crash of October 1929. Unemployment reached about 25 percent. Franklin Roosevelt answered it with the New Deal. For 10 points, name this decade-long economic crisis.

On December 7, 1941, Japanese planes attacked this naval base in Hawaii, sinking or damaging battleships. Franklin Roosevelt called it a "date which will live in infamy." The attack brought the United States into World War II. For 10 points, name this base.

This 1954 Supreme Court case ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional. The NAACP lawyer Thurgood Marshall argued it. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote the unanimous opinion. For 10 points, name this case from Kansas.

In December 1955 this seamstress was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat. Her action sparked a year-long boycott led by Martin Luther King Jr. She worked for the NAACP. For 10 points, name this civil rights icon.

This scandal began with a 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee offices in a Washington building. Reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein investigated it. President Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 because of it. For 10 points, name this scandal.

q: This Frankish king was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day in the year 800. He ruled from Aachen and sponsored a revival of learning known as the Carolingian Renaissance. His grandfather Charles Martel won the Battle of Tours. For 10 points, name this king.

This epidemic killed roughly one-third of Europe's population in the middle of the fourteenth century. It spread along trade routes from Asia and was carried by fleas on rats. Its victims developed swollen lymph nodes called buboes. For 10 points, name this plague.

This teenage peasant girl heard voices she believed came from saints and led French troops to lift the siege of Orleans in 1429. She helped Charles VII reach Reims for his coronation. English-allied judges convicted her of heresy and burned her at Rouen. For 10 points, name this French heroine.

In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II conquered this city, ending the Byzantine Empire. Its defenders were led by Emperor Constantine XI, and its walls were battered by huge cannon. The Hagia Sophia was converted into a mosque. For 10 points, name this city, later renamed Istanbul.

On October 31, 1517, this German monk is said to have posted his Ninety-five Theses at Wittenberg, attacking the sale of indulgences. He was excommunicated and defended himself at the Diet of Worms. He translated the Bible into German. For 10 points, name this founder of Protestantism.

This English king broke with the Roman Catholic Church so he could annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. He had six wives, including Anne Boleyn and Jane Seymour. He founded the Church of England. For 10 points, name this Tudor king.

In 1588 this fleet of about 130 ships sailed from Spain to invade England on behalf of Philip II. English ships and fireships harried it in the Channel, and storms wrecked many vessels as it sailed home around Scotland. Francis Drake and Charles Howard commanded the English ships. For 10 points, name this defeated fleet.

Ended by two treaties signed in 1648, this conflict began with the Defenestration of Prague. It devastated the Holy Roman Empire, and Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden fought in it. The settlement established the principle of state sovereignty in Europe. For 10 points, name this religious war of the early seventeenth century, which lasted three decades.

This French king ruled for seventy-two years and built the Palace of Versailles. He called himself the "Sun King" and is said to have declared "I am the state." He revoked the Edict of Nantes. For 10 points, name this king whose number is fourteen.

After the English Civil War, this Puritan general ruled as Lord Protector. He led the New Model Army and signed the death warrant of Charles I. He closed the theaters and conquered Ireland. For 10 points, name this man who ruled England without a king in the 1650s.

In 1688 William of Orange invaded England and James II fled to France. Parliament offered the crown jointly to William and his wife Mary. The English Bill of Rights followed. For 10 points, name this bloodless event, sometimes called the Revolution of 1688.

This Russian tsar traveled incognito to Western Europe and then built a new capital on the Baltic Sea. He defeated Charles XII of Sweden at Poltava. He forced his nobles to shave their beards. For 10 points, name this tsar called "the Great."

This German-born empress seized power from her husband Peter III in a coup in 1762. She corresponded with Voltaire and expanded Russia's borders into Crimea and Poland. She was called an enlightened despot. For 10 points, name this Russian ruler.

On July 14, 1789, a Parisian crowd stormed this fortress prison, which held few prisoners but a lot of gunpowder. The event became a symbol of the French Revolution and is celebrated as a national holiday. For 10 points, name this Paris fortress.

This lawyer led the Committee of Public Safety during the Reign of Terror. He was called "the Incorruptible" and was himself guillotined in July 1794. He supported the Cult of the Supreme Being. For 10 points, name this Jacobin leader.

This Corsican general crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804. He won at Austerlitz but lost most of his army during an invasion of Russia in 1812. He was exiled to Elba and then to Saint Helena. For 10 points, name this man.

On June 18, 1815, the Duke of Wellington and Prussian forces under Blucher defeated Napoleon at this battle in present-day Belgium. It ended the Hundred Days. For 10 points, name this battle that sent Napoleon to Saint Helena.

This Austrian foreign minister dominated the 1814-1815 Congress of Vienna. He sought a balance of power and the restoration of legitimate monarchs after Napoleon. He later fled Vienna during the 1848 revolutions. For 10 points, name this conservative statesman.

This Italian nationalist led his Red Shirts to conquer Sicily and Naples in 1860 and then handed his conquests to Victor Emmanuel II. He fought in South America before returning to Italy. For 10 points, name this general of the Risorgimento.

This Prussian chancellor unified Germany through the wars with Denmark, Austria, and France. He used "blood and iron" and the Ems Dispatch to provoke war in 1870. Wilhelm I was proclaimed emperor at Versailles in 1871. For 10 points, name this "Iron Chancellor."

This nurse organized care for wounded British soldiers at Scutari during the Crimean War. Called "the Lady with the Lamp," she founded a school of nursing at Saint Thomas' Hospital. For 10 points, name this British reformer.

In June 1914 a Bosnian Serb nationalist named Gavrilo Princip shot this Austrian archduke and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo. The killing triggered a chain of alliances leading to World War I. For 10 points, name this heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne.

This 1919 treaty required Germany to accept responsibility for World War I, pay reparations, and give up territory. It was signed in the Hall of Mirrors. It created the League of Nations. For 10 points, name this treaty that ended the war with Germany.

This Bolshevik leader returned to Russia in April 1917 and led the October Revolution. He founded the Soviet state and introduced the New Economic Policy. For 10 points, name this man, born Vladimir Ulyanov.

This leader of the Nazi Party became chancellor of Germany in 1933. He wrote Mein Kampf, started World War II by invading Poland, and committed suicide in a bunker in Berlin. For 10 points, name this dictator.

In September 1938 Britain's Neville Chamberlain and France's Edouard Daladier agreed at this conference to let Germany annex the Sudetenland. Czechoslovakia was not invited. Chamberlain said it brought "peace for our time." For 10 points, name this conference held in a German city.

In the summer of 1940 the Royal Air Force defended southern England against the Luftwaffe in this air campaign. Radar and Spitfire fighters helped Britain win. Winston Churchill praised "the few." For 10 points, name this battle.
This long Soviet victory of 1942 and 1943 trapped the German Sixth Army under Friedrich Paulus in a city on the Volga. It marked a turning point on the Eastern Front. For 10 points, name this battle.

Led by Dwight Eisenhower, the Allies landed on five beaches in Normandy on June 6, 1944. The beaches were code-named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword. For 10 points, name this invasion, known by a letter and a word.

This 1598 decree issued by Henry IV of France granted Huguenots the right to worship in certain towns. It was revoked by his grandson Louis XIV in 1685, causing many Protestants to flee. It was issued in a city in Brittany. For 10 points, name this edict.

q: This earliest known writing system was pressed into clay tablets with a reed stylus by the people of Sumer. Its wedge-shaped marks were used to record grain and later literature such as the Epic of Gilgamesh. For 10 points, name this writing system whose name means "wedge-shaped."

This Babylonian king issued a law code carved on a black stone stele, which begins with a scene of him before the sun god Shamash. It includes the principle of "an eye for an eye." For 10 points, name this ruler of the early second millennium BC.

These massive tombs were built on the west bank of the Nile near Cairo for kings such as Khufu. The Great one was built around 2500 BC and was the tallest human-made structure for thousands of years. For 10 points, name these Egyptian monuments at Giza.

This official of the Third Dynasty served King Djoser and is credited with designing the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. He was later worshiped as a god of medicine by Greeks. His name means "he who comes in peace." For 10 points, name this Egyptian architect and physician.

This female pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty built a mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri and sent a trade expedition to Punt. She often wore a false beard in statues. Thutmose III later tried to erase her images. For 10 points, name this woman.

This pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty fought the Hittites at Kadesh and built the temples at Abu Simbel. He ruled for about sixty-six years and had many children. For 10 points, name this Egyptian king called "the Great."

This burial ground near Thebes holds the tombs of New Kingdom pharaohs such as Thutmose III and Seti I. Its tombs were cut into cliffs and hidden to deter robbers. Workers lived in the nearby village of Deir el-Medina. For 10 points, name this valley on the west bank of the Nile opposite Luxor.

This pharaoh moved Egypt's capital to Amarna and promoted worship of the sun disk Aten. He was the husband of Nefertiti and likely the father of Tutankhamun. For 10 points, name this pharaoh who changed his name from Amenhotep IV.

This 31 BC naval battle off the western coast of Greece was won by Marcus Agrippa for Octavian. Mark Antony and Cleopatra fled with part of their fleet after it. It left Octavian master of the Roman world. For 10 points, name this battle named for a promontory.

This Bronze Age civilization on Crete built a palace at Knossos with a labyrinth-like plan. Arthur Evans excavated it and named it for a legendary king. It left frescoes of bull-leaping. For 10 points, name this culture.

In this war, according to Homer, a Greek army besieged a city for ten years after Paris took Helen. Odysseus devised a wooden horse to enter the city. For 10 points, name this legendary conflict, fought at a city in Asia Minor.

Themistocles lured the Persian fleet of Xerxes into narrow waters near an island off the coast of Attica in 480 BC. The Greeks had about 370 ships, many of them Athenian triremes. Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore. For 10 points, name this naval battle named for an island.

King Leonidas and his three hundred Spartans held a narrow coastal pass against the Persian army of Xerxes in 480 BC. They were betrayed by Ephialtes, who showed the Persians a mountain path. For 10 points, name this battle.

This alliance was formed in 478 BC with its treasury on a small island, and it was led by Athens against Persia. Its funds were moved to Athens and used to build the Parthenon. Members like Naxos and Thasos were forced to stay. For 10 points, name this league named for its original treasury site.

This war between Athens and Sparta lasted from 431 to 404 BC. Thucydides wrote its history. Athens lost after the failed Sicilian expedition and the defeat at Aegospotami. For 10 points, name this Greek conflict.

This Athenian philosopher was sentenced to death for impiety and corrupting the youth in 399 BC. He drank hemlock. Plato recorded his questioning method in dialogues. For 10 points, name this teacher.

This king of Macedon, tutored by Aristotle, conquered the Persian Empire after winning at Issus and Gaugamela. He founded Alexandria in Egypt and died in Babylon at 32. For 10 points, name this conqueror.

These seafaring people from cities such as Tyre and Sidon spread an alphabet around the Mediterranean and founded Carthage. They were famous for purple dye. For 10 points, name these people of ancient Lebanon.

This founder of the Achaemenid Persian Empire conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed Jews to return to Jerusalem. The Cyrus Cylinder records his policies. For 10 points, name this king, whose title was "the Great."

This Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with elephants during the Second Punic War. He destroyed a Roman army at Cannae in 216 BC. He was finally defeated at Zama by Scipio Africanus. For 10 points, name this general.
In 49 BC this general led his legion across a small river in northern Italy, starting a civil war with Pompey. He said "the die is cast." For 10 points, name this Roman dictator, who named a month.
Born Octavian, this man defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC and became the first Roman emperor. The Senate gave him a title meaning "revered." For 10 points, name this man.

This Roman emperor was blamed by rumor for the fire of 64 AD and blamed the Christians in return. His mother was Agrippina, and his tutor was Seneca. He killed himself in 68. For 10 points, name this last Julio-Claudian emperor.
This Roman city near Naples was buried under volcanic ash in 79 AD when Mount Vesuvius erupted. Its remains preserved homes, mosaics, and the bodies of victims. For 10 points, name this city.
This Roman emperor won the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312. He legalized Christianity with the Edict of Milan and founded a new capital on the Bosporus. For 10 points, name this emperor.

This emperor divided Rome's administration into four parts called the Tetrarchy. He persecuted Christians and later retired to grow cabbages in Dalmatia. For 10 points, name this ruler who took power in 284.
This first emperor of unified China took the throne in 221 BC. He standardized weights and measures and was buried with a terracotta army. For 10 points, name this ruler of the Qin dynasty.

This Mauryan emperor ruled most of the Indian subcontinent in the third century BC. After the bloody Kalinga War he converted to Buddhism and sent missionaries abroad. He had edicts carved on rocks and pillars, some topped with lions. For 10 points, name this emperor.

This gladiator led a slave revolt in 73 BC against the Roman Republic. He escaped from a gladiator school in Capua and defeated several Roman armies. Marcus Crassus finally defeated his forces. His followers were crucified along the Appian Way. For 10 points, name this man.

q: This Roman orator held the consulship in 63 BC and exposed the conspiracy of Catiline. His speeches against Mark Antony were called the Philippics. Antony's agents killed him in 43 BC. For 10 points, name this author of On the Republic and many letters.

This Chinese poet of the Tang dynasty is known for drinking, nature poems, and Quiet Night Thought. His friend Du Fu is also a major Tang poet. Tradition says he drowned trying to embrace the moon. For 10 points, name this poet.

This African leader spent 27 years in prison before becoming South Africa's first Black president in 1994. He shared a Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk. He led the African National Congress. For 10 points, name this man.

This Mongol leader united the steppe tribes in 1206 and took a title that means "universal ruler." His armies conquered Central Asia and northern China. He died in 1227. For 10 points, name this founder of the Mongol Empire.

This grandson of Genghis Khan completed the Mongol conquest of China and founded the Yuan dynasty. He moved his capital to what is now Beijing. Marco Polo claimed to have visited his court. For 10 points, name this Mongol ruler.

This Chinese admiral led seven great treasure voyages in the early fifteenth century for the Ming emperor. His fleet reached India and East Africa. He was a Muslim eunuch from Yunnan. For 10 points, name this man.
This ruler of the Mali Empire made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and gave out so much gold that its price dropped in Cairo. He built a mosque in Timbuktu. For 10 points, name this king.
This West African empire rose after Mali and was ruled by Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad. It had Gao as a capital and fell to a Moroccan army armed with guns in 1591. For 10 points, name this empire.

This Ottoman sultan, called "the Magnificent," took Belgrade and Rhodes and besieged Vienna in 1529. He codified laws and was known in his own country as "the Lawgiver." The Ottoman Empire reached its height under him. For 10 points, name this sultan.

This Mughal emperor ruled from 1556 to 1605 and expanded his empire across northern India. He promoted religious tolerance and abolished a tax on non-Muslims. He built the capital of Fatehpur Sikri. For 10 points, name this grandson of Babur.

This mausoleum has four minarets, a large central dome, and a long reflecting pool. It took about twenty years to build in the seventeenth century and holds the tomb of Mumtaz Mahal. Its builder was later imprisoned by his son Aurangzeb. For 10 points, name this white marble tomb in Agra.

Officers on four "black ships" under this man arrived in Edo Bay in 1853 carrying a letter from President Millard Fillmore. He returned the next year, and Japan signed the Treaty of Kanagawa. He was a younger brother of a hero of the War of 1812. For 10 points, name this American commodore.

This 1868 event restored the emperor of Japan to power and ended the shogunate. It brought rapid industrialization and a modern army. It was named for the emperor's reign title. For 10 points, name this period.
Britain fought China in this conflict from 1839 to 1842 after Lin Zexu seized chests of a drug. The Treaty of Nanjing gave Britain Hong Kong. For 10 points, name this war named for a narcotic.
Led by Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be Jesus's brother, this rebellion killed millions in China between 1850 and 1864. It set up a "Heavenly Kingdom" in Nanjing. For 10 points, name this rebellion.

This 1857 revolt began when Indian soldiers in the East India Company's army refused to use cartridges greased with animal fat. It started in Meerut and spread to Delhi and Kanpur. For 10 points, name this uprising, also called the First War of Independence.

In 1930 this Indian leader marched about 240 miles to the sea at Dandi to make salt in defiance of British law. He led the independence movement with nonviolent resistance. For 10 points, name this man.
In 1947 British India was split into two countries along religious lines, causing massive migration and violence. Cyril Radcliffe drew the boundary. For 10 points, name this event.

This leader proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949 after winning the civil war against the Nationalists. He led the Long March and later began the Cultural Revolution. For 10 points, name this Communist leader.
This Chinese campaign of 1958 to 1962 tried to rapidly industrialize by using communes and backyard steel furnaces. A famine killed tens of millions. For 10 points, name this disastrous campaign.
This 1950 to 1953 war began when North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel. General Douglas MacArthur led United Nations forces, and Chinese troops intervened. For 10 points, name this war.
In 1954 the Viet Minh under General Vo Nguyen Giap defeated French forces at this fortress in northwestern Vietnam. The Geneva Accords then divided the country. For 10 points, name this battle.

This South African system of legal racial segregation began in 1948. Nelson Mandela was imprisoned for opposing it. Its laws included pass laws and the Group Areas Act. For 10 points, name this system.

This king united his people in southern Africa in the early 1800s and ruled from his capital at kwaBulawayo. He used short stabbing spears and the "buffalo horns" formation. The upheaval of his wars is called the Mfecane. For 10 points, name this Zulu king.

Hosted by a German chancellor, this 1884 and 1885 meeting set rules for European claims in Africa, including the requirement of effective occupation. No African leaders attended. It recognized the Congo Free State of King Leopold II. For 10 points, name this meeting that helped spark the Scramble for Africa.
In 1956 Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized this waterway, leading Britain, France, and Israel to attack. For 10 points, name this canal connecting the Mediterranean and Red Seas.

This man studied in the United States and Britain before returning home to lead his own political party. He became prime minister in 1957 when his country broke from British rule. He was a leading advocate of pan-Africanism and was overthrown in a coup while visiting China. For 10 points, name this first leader of Ghana.

This 1979 upheaval overthrew a monarch who had been restored in a 1953 coup. Strikes and mass demonstrations forced the shah to flee. An exiled cleric returned from Paris and an Islamic republic was proclaimed. For 10 points, name this revolution that brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power.

This concubine of the Xianfeng Emperor became regent for her son and then her nephew and controlled the Qing court for almost fifty years. She backed the Boxers in 1900 and blocked the Hundred Days Reform of 1898. She died in 1908 just one day after the emperor she had imprisoned. For 10 points, name this empress dowager.
This doctor and revolutionary helped overthrow the Qing dynasty in 1911. He became provisional president of the Republic of China and founded the Kuomintang. For 10 points, name this man.

This shogunate ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868 from Edo, now Tokyo. It limited foreign trade to the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki and expelled missionaries. Its founder won the Battle of Sekigahara. For 10 points, name this family of shoguns, founded by Ieyasu.

q: This Mexican revolutionary from Morelos led peasants under the slogan "Land and Liberty." His Plan of Ayala demanded the return of village lands. He was ambushed and killed at Chinameca in 1919. For 10 points, name this southern leader of the Mexican Revolution.

This Mexican revolutionary led the Division of the North and raided Columbus, New Mexico, in 1916. General John Pershing chased him without capturing him. He was assassinated in 1923. For 10 points, name this man, whose real name was Doroteo Arango.

This Zapotec lawyer served as president of Mexico and resisted the French intervention under Maximilian. His 1859 Reform Laws separated church and state. For 10 points, name this man whose birthday is a national holiday in Mexico.

This Mexican general and president lost Texas after being captured at San Jacinto in 1836. He had earlier led the siege of the Alamo. He lost the Mexican-American War and was exiled several times. For 10 points, name this man who held the presidency eleven times.

This woman was the wife of Argentine president Juan Peron and led a foundation for the poor. She campaigned for women's suffrage, which passed in 1947. She died of cancer in 1952 at age thirty-three. For 10 points, name this woman, whose nickname was "Evita."

This Argentine doctor joined Fidel Castro's guerrillas and helped win the Cuban Revolution. He later tried to start revolts in the Congo and Bolivia, where he was executed in 1967. For 10 points, name this man whose image appears on many T-shirts.

In April 1961 about 1,400 Cuban exiles trained by the CIA landed on Cuba's southern coast at a bay of this name. President Kennedy refused air support, and Fidel Castro's forces crushed the landing. For 10 points, name this failed invasion.
In 1970 this physician became Chile's first democratically elected Marxist president. He died during a 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet. For 10 points, name this Chilean president.
